ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Two parallel smooth copper rods are inclined at an angle of $\theta = 45^\circ$ to the horizontal. Their upper ends are connected to a power supply and a sliding rheostat, and they are placed in a vertically downward uniform magnetic field. By adjusting the sliding rheostat R, when the ammeter reads $I = 2.5\mathrm{A}$, the aluminum rod placed horizontally on the copper rods remains stationary. The mass of the aluminum rod is $M = 0.2\mathrm{kg}$, and the distance between the two rods is $L = 0.4\mathrm{m}$.

1. What is the magnetic induction intensity $B$? (Assume $g = 10 \, \mathrm{m}/\mathrm{s}^2$)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description first: The attached diagram shows two parallel inclined conducting rails on a slope, with an aluminum rod bridging the rails. The upper part is connected into an external circuit containing a power supply/sliding rheostat arrangement and an ammeter marked A. Several vertical downward arrows are drawn and labeled B, indicating a uniform magnetic field directed downward. The rod is shown placed horizontally across the inclined rails, and the incline angle is represented relative to a dashed horizontal reference. Reasoning: Treat the aluminum rod as the object in equilibrium on the smooth inclined rails, so friction is absent. The given data are I = 2.5 A, M = 0.2 kg, L = 0.4 m, θ = 45°, and g = 10 m/s². Because the rod is horizontal while the magnetic field is vertical, the current-carrying rod experiences a horizontal magnetic force of magnitude F = BIL. For the rod to remain stationary along the inclined rails, the upslope component of this horizontal magnetic force must balance the downslope component of gravity. The gravitational component along the rails is Mg sin θ. The component of the horizontal magnetic force along the rails is F cos θ = BIL cos θ. Thus equilibrium gives BIL cos θ = Mg sin θ. Therefore B = Mg tan θ/(IL). Substituting values: B = (0.2 × 10 × tan45°)/(2.5 × 0.4) = (2 × 1)/1 = 2 T.
